lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Add the full protocol to the portfolio URL.
items.because: The current form may not be recognized as a clickable link by resume parsers.

items.says: Label the code profile or use a destination that makes clear what it contains.
Make linked research code, publications, packages, or projects available and documented.
Consider adding a LinkedIn, Google Scholar, ORCID, or publications link.
items.because: A code link alone may undersell the research profile for a statistics or quant role.

items.says: Use the university’s official degree notation.
items.because: The program’s designation may differ from “Ph.D. candidate in Statistics.”

items.says: Add a dissertation title, research area, advisor, or short research-focus line if relevant.
items.because: The doctoral specialization is otherwise unclear.

items.says: Clarify whether qualifying exams have been passed or candidacy has been reached, if relevant.
items.because: “Ph.D. candidate” can mean different things to different employers.

items.says: Keep the expected graduation date current.
Add honors, GPA, concentration, or coursework only if strong and relevant.
items.because: At this stage, coursework matters less than research and experience.

items.says: Consider grouping the two degrees under one university heading.
items.because: It would reduce repetition and save space.

items.says: Make the education and research-assistant timeline clear.
items.because: The review flags a possible apparent gap between the bachelor’s degree and doctorate.

items.says: Lead with the most relevant research and make the bakery role visually secondary to Northpeak.
items.because: The bakery role is less relevant to quant research and takes space from stronger work.

items.says: Keep the résumé to one or two pages.
items.because: The review recommends that length for a quantitative research, statistics, or machine-learning role.

items.says: Shorten or omit the bakery role for a quant-focused résumé unless it serves a clear purpose.
items.because: It is less relevant than the research work.

items.says: Verify that the bakery dates do not create an unexplained overlap.
items.because: The role may overlap another position or academic commitment.

items.says: Use consistent American or British spelling for “labour.”
items.because: The review says the rest of the résumé uses American conventions.

items.says: Clarify the scale of the weekly labour budget.
items.because: “Within budget” does not show the size or difficulty of the responsibility.

items.says: Consider omitting “opening shifts” for quant applications.
items.because: It is more useful for operations roles.

items.says: Clarify the measurement period and whether the reduction was sustained.
items.because: A short-term improvement could sound less robust.

items.says: Explain how “unsold bread” was calculated if needed.
items.because: The metric may not be self-evident.

items.says: Consider omitting this bullet if space is limited on a quant résumé.
items.because: It mainly demonstrates process improvement and data-informed decision-making.

items.says: Identify the internship’s desk or asset class if permissible.
items.because: That context would make the role clearer.

items.says: Confirm performance claims are approved for external use.
items.because: Sharpe ratios, trading signals, and desk results can be sensitive even when anonymized.

items.says: Clarify whether the signal alone or its addition to an existing portfolio produced the Sharpe increase.
items.because: The wording could imply that the signal caused the entire portfolio improvement.

items.says: State the annualization convention, risk-free-rate assumption, and scope of costs.
items.because: Those details matter for a substantial Sharpe improvement.

items.says: Specify the out-of-sample validation design.
items.because: “Out-of-sample” alone is not enough for a quant reviewer.

items.says: Ensure the 18-month test period did not overlap training or parameter selection.
Clarify what the 90% return-retention figure measures.
items.because: “Keeping 90% of gross returns” can be interpreted ambiguously.

items.says: Specify whether turnover is one-way or two-way and how it is measured.
Say whether the slippage reduction was modeled or observed in execution data.
items.because: The distinction affects credibility.

items.says: Make the three percentages’ baselines and periods compatible and clear.
Reduce the bullet’s metric density.
items.because: Its denominators are currently ambiguous.

items.says: Define the metric behind “forecast gain.”
items.because: It could mean lower QLIKE, lower MSE, improved directional accuracy, or something else.

items.says: Explain how multiple comparisons across 30 indices were handled.
items.because: Unadjusted tests for each index can overstate significance.

items.says: State whether the test used a small-sample correction and an appropriate variance estimator.
items.because: These choices matter especially if forecasts overlap.

items.says: Verify that standard Diebold–Mariano tests suit the nested-model setting.
items.because: They can be inappropriate or biased in some nested-model settings.

items.says: Fix the feature-store bullet’s grammatical construction.
items.because: The opening participle does not connect cleanly to the subject.

items.says: Clarify whether you built the feature store individually or contributed to a team effort.
Explain what “point-in-time” means here.
items.because: It could refer to look-ahead prevention, timestamp alignment, or historical feature availability.

items.says: Quantify the feature store’s engineering impact if possible.
items.because: Preparation time, reproducibility, or data failures could show its value.

items.says: Make the feature-store bullet less technically dense.
items.because: It is difficult to parse as written.

items.says: Annualizing daily Sharpe by multiplying by 252 is incorrect.
items.because: A daily-return Sharpe ratio is generally multiplied by the square root of 252; multiplying by 252 substantially overstates it.

items.says: Clarify whether the next cohort’s use of the wiki was measured or observed.
items.because: The onboarding claim may be difficult to verify.

items.says: Trim the list of documentation topics or show a clearer practical outcome.
items.because: The bullet lists several topics but little outcome beyond onboarding.

items.says: Add a relevant faculty member, lab website, or research area.
items.because: The lab’s focus could be more informative than the generic role title.

items.says: Explain what caused the simulation speed improvement.
items.because: Parallelization, vectorization, or scheduling details would show engineering depth.

items.says: Check that the controls support “every run reproducible.”
items.because: Software versions, random-number behavior, data inputs, and configuration files must be controlled.

items.says: Say whether others reused the pipeline.
items.because: Reuse would strengthen its impact.

items.says: Specify what improvement “by a log factor” means.
items.because: Improving by a multiplicative logarithmic term and removing a logarithmic factor are materially different.

items.says: Add the paper title, coauthors, preprint, or DOI link if available.
items.because: The work is under review, not accepted or published.

items.says: Confirm that the JASA review status and use of the journal name are accurate and permitted.
Identify the estimator or theoretical setting if useful.
items.because: The claim may be too abstract for nonacademic recruiters.

items.says: Give the teaching rating’s response context.
items.because: An evaluation based on only a subset of students can be misleading.

items.says: De-emphasize the problem-set count or omit the bullet if space is limited.
items.because: Teaching strengthens a quant-research application less directly than the research and engineering bullets.

items.says: Split the package release from the lab’s administrative duties or remove less relevant duties.
items.because: The bullet combines software release, systems administration, reading-group organization, and grading.

items.says: Make the package the unmistakable subject of the download statistic.
items.because: “Which was downloaded” has an ambiguous antecedent.

items.says: Link the package and identify its repository or package index.
Define what the 3,000 downloads count represents.
items.because: Total downloads and unique installations have substantially different meanings.

items.says: Verify that the package remains accessible, documented, tested, and installable.
Explain how this project differs from the Northpeak internship or reduce one section.
items.because: The two entries overlap heavily and may look like the same project twice.

items.says: Clarify whether the project shares data, features, a baseline, or a model family with the internship.
items.because: Reviewers may otherwise wonder whether the results are duplicated.

items.says: Link any paper, preprint, presentation, or public repository from the project.
Update “Present” if the project is no longer active.
Include the data source and evaluation design if space allows.
items.because: Financial forecasting results are sensitive to leakage and validation choices.

items.says: Specify whether the 7% result is averaged, median, or pooled across indices.
Say whether the result is statistically significant or only a point estimate.
Describe the out-of-sample split or rolling evaluation design.
items.because: It is essential to a time-series claim.

items.says: Say whether HAR-RV had the same information constraints and evaluation period.
items.because: The baseline comparison needs to be comparable.

items.says: Avoid repeating the baseline and 30-index result in other bullets without a distinct contribution.
Define “forecast error.”
items.because: It could mean QLIKE, RMSE, MAE, or another metric.

items.says: A drop from 0.20 to 0.15 is not a 33% baseline-relative improvement.
items.because: It is a 25% reduction relative to 0.20.

items.says: Distinguish this result from the preceding QLIKE claim or use only one.
items.because: Both bullets may describe the same metric and evaluation setting.

items.says: Separate the effects of added features and the asymmetric loss.
items.because: Attributing the gain to both may require ablation studies.

items.says: Calling the move from 52% to 58% a 6% improvement uses incorrect percentage terminology.
items.because: It is a 6-percentage-point increase, or about an 11.5% relative increase.

items.says: Say whether the hit rates are pooled, averaged across indices, or calculated another way.
Explain the target’s economic meaning and the effects of costs or class imbalance.
items.because: They affect how the hit rate should be interpreted.

items.says: Reduce repetition of the model and 30-index evaluation.
items.because: Earlier project bullets already describe them.

items.says: Do not give the hit-rate result equal prominence unless it is significant.
items.because: It may not be statistically or economically significant.

items.says: Give the competition’s exact name if recognizable.
Link the competition profile or solution write-up if available.
Make the individual contribution clear rather than relying on “Team of 3.”
items.because: Team structure alone does not show what you did.

items.says: Limit the competition’s space if it was not financial or time-series related.
items.because: More relevant work should take priority.

items.says: Consider a more precise percentile than “top 2%.”
items.because: Rank 41 of 2,900 is approximately the top 1.4%, though top 2% is broadly true.

items.says: Clarify that the ranking is the team’s final private-leaderboard result.
items.because: The competition may also have had a public leaderboard.

items.says: State your specific contribution to the ensemble.
items.because: It was a team effort.

items.says: Describe the change as improving the validation design rather than directly measuring reduced leakage.
items.because: “Cut leakage” is not normally a directly measured quantity.

items.says: Identify the metric behind the 0.02 gap and whether it narrowed consistently.
items.because: One split may not establish a sustained improvement.

items.says: Explain that the folds mirrored the competition’s temporal structure.
items.because: That would strengthen the methodological point.

items.says: Avoid implying the leaderboard gap proves leakage was eliminated.
items.because: The gap alone does not establish that.

items.says: Clarify whether feature selection occurred within each training fold.
items.because: Using all data for permutation importance before validation could introduce leakage.

items.says: Say whether validation score was unchanged exactly or within a tolerance.
items.because: Exact equality may sound implausible.

items.says: Separate languages, frameworks, and infrastructure tools.
items.because: They are different kinds of skills, not equivalent programming entries.

items.says: Show how Kafka was used or remove it.
items.because: The experience bullets do not currently demonstrate it.

items.says: Classify PyTorch as a framework rather than a programming language.
Add relevant tools such as SQL, Git, Linux, cloud, or numerical libraries only if used materially.
items.because: The listed work may support more specific tool claims.

items.says: Correct the misspelling “econometircs.”
Use consistent capitalization and terminology.
Organize the methods by category.
items.because: Gradient boosting is a model family, while the other entries are broader areas.

items.says: List more specific methods demonstrated elsewhere on the résumé.
items.because: The experience supports a more specific and credible methods section.
